name: AI for Productivity and Operations
objectives: Given a messy to-do list and your real available hours, create a prioritized day-by-day weekly plan with AI, with the top three tasks blocked on your calendar

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Planning your week with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Turn a messy to-do list into a prioritized weekly plan.
This lesson builds toward: Given a messy to-do list and your real available hours, you will create a prioritized day-by-day weekly plan with AI, with the top three tasks blocked on your calendar.
A long, mixed-up to-do list makes everything feel urgent. AI can sort it fast. Dump every task into the chat, then ask it to sort and plan.
A useful prompt: "Here is my to-do list for the week. Sort it into: must do this week, should do, can wait, and can hand off. Then make a day-by-day plan. I have about 3 hours a day for office work, and Tuesday is busy with deliveries."
You are the boss of the plan. Move anything the AI got wrong, block time on your calendar for the top three tasks, and leave room for surprises.
Step by step:
- Write every task, big and small, in one list.
- Ask AI to sort it into must, should, can wait and hand off.
- Tell it your real available hours and busy days.
- Fix the plan, then block time on your calendar for the top three.
Words to know:
- Prioritize: decide what matters most and do it first.
- Delegate: hand a task to someone else.
Try it now: Write your full to-do list for this week. Ask an AI assistant to sort it and make a day-by-day plan using your real hours, then fix it and block your top three tasks on a calendar.
You can now turn a messy to-do list into a prioritized weekly plan with AI.

check.q: In this course's weekly plan, what does "hand off" mean?
options: Tasks that must be done today
check.why: Hand-off tasks are ones someone else can do.

check.q: AI's plan puts your biggest task on Tuesday, your busiest delivery day. What do you do?
options: Ask AI for a new list of tasks
Move the task to a quieter day and block that time on your calendar
check.why: You are the boss of the plan; fix what the AI got wrong.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Writing a standard operating procedure
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Turn how you do a task into a clear, step-by-step procedure anyone can follow.
This lesson builds toward: For a task your organization repeats, you will write a numbered standard operating procedure with purpose, supplies, steps, safety notes and a checklist, so a new person can follow it without stopping.
A standard operating procedure (SOP) is written steps for a repeated task: opening the shop, cleaning the kitchen, checking in a client, counting the cash drawer. With an SOP, new staff or volunteers learn faster and things get done the same way every time.
The fastest way: talk or type it out the way you would explain it to a new person, even if messy. Then ask AI: "Turn this into a numbered SOP with a title, purpose, supplies needed, steps of one action each, safety notes and a final checklist. Use simple words."
Test it: have someone who has never done the task follow it while you watch quietly. Every time they hesitate, the SOP needs a clearer step. Date it and say who owns it.
Step by step:
- Explain the task out loud or in writing, messy is fine.
- Ask AI to turn it into a numbered SOP with purpose, supplies, steps, safety notes and a checklist.
- Check each step for accuracy.
- Have a new person test it.
- Fix unclear steps, then date it and name an owner.
Words to know:
- SOP: standard operating procedure: written steps for a repeated task.
- Checklist: a list of items to tick off so nothing is missed.
Try it now: Pick one task you do every week. Explain it in your own words, have AI turn it into an SOP, check it, and ask someone to try following it.
You can now write and test a clear standard operating procedure with AI help.

check.why: An SOP is a standard operating procedure: written steps for a repeated task.

check.q: Your AI-made SOP for closing the shop says "lock up" but skips the back door. What do you do?
options: Check each step for accuracy and add the missing step
Let new staff figure it out
check.why: Check every step for accuracy before anyone uses the SOP.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Turning meetings into action items
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Run a short meeting and use AI to turn notes into decisions and action items.
This lesson builds toward: After a short meeting, you will list the decisions, action items and open questions from the notes, with every action item having an agreed owner and due date, sent within a day.
Many meetings end with everyone nodding and nothing happening. The fix is simple: every meeting ends with action items, each with an owner and a due date.
Use an agenda with times. Take quick notes, or use a meeting tool's built-in AI notes if your organization allows it and everyone has been told. Then paste the notes into AI: "From these notes, list decisions made, action items with owner and due date, and open questions."
Check the list before sending, because AI may guess an owner or date that was never agreed. Remove anything private, such as staff health or pay details, before sharing. Send it within a day.
Step by step:
- Write a short agenda with times.
- Take notes or use approved AI notes, with everyone informed.
- Ask AI to pull out decisions, action items and open questions.
- Check owners and dates; remove private details.
- Send the action list within a day.
Words to know:
- Agenda: the list of topics for a meeting, in order.
- Action item: a task from a meeting with an owner and a due date.
Try it now: Take notes at your next meeting, or write notes from a recent one. Use AI to pull out decisions and action items with owners and dates, check them, and write the message you would send.
You can now turn meeting notes into checked action items with owners and due dates.

check.q: What makes a meeting end with real follow-through?
options: Action items, each with an owner and a due date
check.why: Action items with owners and dates turn talk into work.

check.q: Your meeting notes mention a staff member's medical leave. What do you do before sharing the AI summary?
options: Post it on the notice board
check.why: Remove private details, such as health or pay, before sharing notes.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Building a staff or volunteer schedule
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use AI and a spreadsheet to build a fair one-week schedule that covers every shift.
This lesson builds toward: Given shifts, availability and rules, you will create a one-week staff or volunteer schedule that covers every shift, following your hour limits, required skills and labor rules.
Scheduling is a puzzle: who is available, which shifts need how many people, and who has which skills. AI can draft a first version in seconds.
Give it the rules without private details: "Make a one-week schedule table. Shifts: Mon-Fri 8-12 and 12-4, two people each. Saturday 9-1, three people. Availability: Person A weekdays only, Person B not Mondays... Each person no more than 20 hours. At least one person with food-handler training per shift."
Check the draft against your rules and any labor laws that apply, such as breaks and minors' hours; your state labor department lists them. Put the final schedule in a shared spreadsheet so everyone sees changes.
Step by step:
- List shifts and how many people each needs.
- List each person's availability using first names or labels.
- List rules: maximum hours, required skills.
- Ask AI for a schedule table.
- Check rules and labor laws, then share it in a spreadsheet.
Words to know:
- Shift: a set block of work time.
- Availability: the times a person can work or volunteer.
Try it now: Write the shifts, availability and rules for a real or practice team of at least four people. Have AI draft a week's schedule, check every rule, and fix any problems.
You can now build and check a fair weekly schedule with AI help.

check.q: What should you give AI when asking for a schedule?
options: Shifts, first names or labels, availability and rules
check.why: AI needs shifts, availability and rules, but no private details.

check.q: AI's schedule leaves Saturday with no one who has food-handler training. What do you do?
options: Change it so every shift has a trained person
Keep it; it is only one day
Ask the untrained staff to guess
check.why: Check the draft against every rule, including required skills.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Tracking supplies and reorders
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Build a supplies sheet with reorder points so you never run out.
This lesson builds toward: Given your supplies and how fast you use them, you will build a supplies sheet with reorder points and a formula that flags REORDER, with a reorder point for every item.
Running out of cups, gloves, flour or diapers stops the work. A simple supplies sheet prevents it. Columns: item, unit, amount on hand, weekly use, reorder point, reorder amount and supplier.
The reorder point is the amount that tells you to order now. A simple rule: weekly use times the number of weeks delivery takes, plus a little extra. If you use 10 boxes a week and delivery takes 1 week, reorder at about 12 boxes.
Ask AI for a formula that flags items to reorder: "In Google Sheets, write a formula that shows REORDER when on-hand is at or below the reorder point." Count supplies on the same day each week and update the sheet.
Step by step:
- List items with unit and supplier.
- Estimate weekly use for each.
- Set a reorder point: weekly use x delivery weeks + a little extra.
- Ask AI for a formula that flags REORDER.
- Count every week on the same day.
Words to know:
- Inventory: the supplies or products you have on hand.
- Reorder point: the amount that tells you it is time to order more.
Try it now: Build a supplies sheet with at least eight items, set reorder points, and add an AI-written formula that flags items to reorder.
You can now track supplies with reorder points and an automatic reorder flag.

options: The amount on hand that tells you to order now
check.why: The reorder point is the amount that tells you to order more.

check.q: You use 20 packs of gloves a week and delivery takes 1 week. About when should you reorder?
options: When you have about 22 to 24 packs
check.why: Weekly use times delivery weeks, plus a little extra, gives about 22 to 24 packs.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Reviewing the week and improving
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a short end-of-week review and choose one improvement.
This lesson builds toward: At the end of the week, you will write a short review of wins, misses and problems and choose one improvement, in about 15 minutes, with the improvement added to next week's plan.
A 15-minute review at the end of each week keeps small problems from growing. Look at what got done, what did not, what went wrong, and what to change.
Give AI your plan, your finished action items and a few notes, then ask: "Write a short weekly operations review: wins, misses, problems, and one improvement for next week." Edit it so it is true and fair to your team.
Pick only one improvement per week, such as a new SOP, a schedule fix or a reorder change. Small weekly fixes add up to a much smoother operation over a few months.
Step by step:
- Gather your weekly plan, action items and notes.
- Ask AI for a short review: wins, misses, problems, one improvement.
- Edit it for truth and fairness.
- Choose one improvement and add it to next week's plan.
Words to know:
- Review: a look back to learn what worked and what did not.
- Continuous improvement: making small changes regularly to get better over time.
Try it now: Final task: write your end-of-week review with AI help and choose one improvement. Together with your weekly plan, SOP, action items, schedule and supplies sheet, this completes your weekly operations kit.
You can now run a week of operations with AI help and keep improving it.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Weekly plan Tasks are not sorted, or the plan ignores real available hours. Tasks sorted into must, should, can wait and hand off, with a day-by-day plan that fits real hours. The top three tasks are blocked on a calendar with room left for surprises. Standard operating procedure Steps are vague or out of order, or there is no checklist. Title, purpose, supplies, numbered one-action steps, safety notes, checklist, date and owner. A new person tested it and unclear steps were fixed. Meeting action items Action items have no owner or due date. Decisions, action items with agreed owners and dates, and open questions, with private details removed. Sent within a day, with a check that guessed owners or dates were corrected. Schedule A shift is uncovered or a rule is broken. Every shift covered, hour limits and skills followed, shared in a spreadsheet. Notes the labor rules checked with the state labor department. Supplies sheet No reorder points. Every item has weekly use, a reorder point and a formula that flags REORDER. Includes the supplier and a set day each week to count. Weekly review No review, or no improvement chosen. A short, fair review of wins, misses and problems with one improvement. The improvement is already in next week's plan. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What does an end-of-week review cover?
options: Wins, misses, problems and one improvement
check.why: A short review covers wins, misses, problems and one improvement.

check.q: AI's review blames one volunteer for a late delivery that was the supplier's fault. What do you do?
options: Edit it so it is true and fair to the team
check.why: Edit the AI draft so it is true and fair before sharing it.
